statement: As described in a narrative review by the researchers who ran the studies it summarizes (Greenwald et al., 2014, read from the corrected proof), so that every figure here is second-hand, daily buprenorphine under the tongue, compared with placebo, went with fewer of the brain's µ-opioid receptors free to bind a tracer in PET scans, falling as the dose rose, in people dependent on heroin who were not in treatment; responses to heroin and to hydromorphone, another opioid, were reduced but not abolished at the doses studied; and after a daily 16 mg was stopped, the share of free receptors rose over the three days measured. The authors speak of 'availability' (the share of receptors free) rather than 'occupancy', which cannot be measured directly in people; a fall in availability equals a rise in occupancy only if receptor affinity and the body's own opioids stay constant. Scans began 4 hours after the daily dose, the earliest time studied, which the authors say probably misses the largest fall. In 3 men given 2 mg, then 16 mg, then placebo, double blind (Zubieta et al., 2000), availability against placebo ranged across brain regions from 50% to 64% at 2 mg a day and from 5% to 21% at 16 mg, and withdrawal and heroin-craving scores fell as the dose rose. In 5 volunteers given 32, 16, 2 and 0 mg a day for 12 days each (Greenwald et al., 2003), the regional means were 53% to 72% at 2 mg, 9% to 20% at 16 mg and 2% to 12% at 32 mg; urine tests showed that they kept using opioids between inpatient stays, even at 32 mg a day. In 7 volunteers taking buprenorphine with naloxone (2/0.5, 8/2 and 32/8 mg a day, 14 days each) and tested 15 hours after the dose, against a separate group of 8 on placebo (Comer et al., 2005), self-administration of the larger heroin doses offered decreased only modestly at each maintenance dose, when receptor availability, estimated by a model from behaviour rather than imaged, was 21%, 11% and 6%; the authors' re-analysis suggests that nearly all receptors would have to be occupied, beyond what 32 mg a day achieved, to suppress heroin self-administration fully, and in another of their studies 16 mg a day, or 32 mg every other day, did not fully block the reinforcing effect of injected hydromorphone (Greenwald et al., 2002). The review mentions people who try to get past the block with larger amounts of other opioids, but it reports no data on what happens when they do. In 10 volunteers stabilized on 16 mg a day and then switched, double blind, to placebo (Greenwald et al., 2007), scans 4, 28, 52 and 76 hours after the last dose gave availability of 27% to 31%, 54% to 61%, 65% to 75% and 77% to 94%, against the placebo condition of the 2003 study (other people); after the authors adjusted the 4-hour values to the 2003 study, their fitted curves give 13% to 25% at 4 hours, 37% to 46% at 24 hours, 56% to 73% at 48 hours and 75% to 90% at 72 hours (values between scans are read from the curves, and the adjusted 4-hour range does not match the 2003 study's 9% to 20%). In the same study, the subjective effects of injected hydromorphone were significantly smaller at 4 and 28 hours than at 52 and 76 hours, a recovery the authors call modest. The review's abstract states as results that suppressing withdrawal appears to need 50% availability or less, and that blocking the reinforcing and subjective effects of typical doses of other opioids needs less than 20% (less than 10% against higher-than-usual doses); but its body says that there is no agreed definition of a block and that the availability needed for either effect is not known, its summary says that blockade 'has not been reliably observed under BUP dosing conditions studied to date', and the 20% figure comes from preliminary modelling. The volunteers were relatively healthy, mostly men, aged 18 to 50, without depressive, psychotic or anxiety disorders or substance use disorders other than nicotine, and dependent on heroin; the authors call it unclear whether the findings apply to people seeking treatment or dependent on other opioids; fentanyl was not studied; the scans used buprenorphine without naloxone, although the authors cite data that products under the tongue with and without naloxone have similar effects; and the review reports no results on breathing or overdose, so it says nothing about the risk of overdose when other opioids are used on or after buprenorphine. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: Does Suboxone block other opioids, and for how long? Only partly, in the small laboratory studies summarized in one review by the researchers who ran them. In brain scans of people dependent on heroin who were not in treatment, buprenorphine (the main medicine in Suboxone) took up more of the brain's opioid receptors the higher the daily dose: at 16 mg a day, only about 9 to 20 in 100 receptors were still free 4 hours after the dose. Even so, heroin and another opioid, hydromorphone, still had some effect at the highest doses tested, and the volunteers kept using opioids between their hospital stays. The review mentions people who take larger amounts of other opioids to get past the block, but it has no data on what happens when they do. After 10 volunteers stopped 16 mg a day, the share of free receptors rose steadily over the 3 days of scans, from about 13 to 25 in 100 at 4 hours to about 75 to 90 in 100 at 3 days, and an injected opioid was blunted more at 4 and 28 hours than at 52 and 76 hours. The review's summary names receptor levels needed to block other opioids, but its authors say nobody knows them and that a full block was never reliably seen. The studies had 3 to 10 people each, mostly men, all dependent on heroin; fentanyl was not studied, and the review reports nothing on breathing or overdose.
population: People dependent on heroin who were not seeking treatment, studied as inpatients in laboratory studies by the review's authors, as described in one narrative review: 3 men (Zubieta et al., 2000), 5 volunteers (Greenwald et al., 2003), 10 volunteers (Greenwald et al., 2007; 5 heavier and 5 lighter smokers) and 7 volunteers on buprenorphine with naloxone against a separate group of 8 on placebo (Comer et al., 2005); in the scan studies aged 18 to 50, many fewer women than men, relatively healthy, without depressive, psychotic or anxiety disorders or substance use disorders other than nicotine
exposure: Daily sublingual buprenorphine given by the investigators (study conditions: a liquid at 2 and 16 mg a day in Zubieta et al., 2000; buprenorphine-only tablets at 32, 16 and 2 mg a day, 12 days each, in Greenwald et al., 2003; 16 mg a day for at least 14 days, then placebo, in Greenwald et al., 2007; buprenorphine with naloxone at 2/0.5, 8/2 and 32/8 mg a day, 14 days each, in Comer et al., 2005), with test doses of intranasal heroin or injected hydromorphone given by the investigators; and time since the last dose after stopping 16 mg a day
comparator: Placebo in the same people (Zubieta et al., 2000; Greenwald et al., 2003; doses given in a fixed order); the placebo condition of the 2003 study, in other people (Greenwald et al., 2007); a separate group of 8 heroin-detoxified volunteers on placebo (Comer et al., 2005); earlier against later times after the last dose
outcome: Brain µ-opioid receptor availability (the share free to bind the PET tracer [11C]-carfentanil, as a percentage of placebo) 4 hours after the daily dose or 4 to 76 hours after the last dose; receptor availability estimated by a model from heroin self-administration and ratings (Comer et al., 2005); self-administration and subjective effects of heroin or hydromorphone; the availability thresholds for suppressing withdrawal and for blocking other opioids that the authors infer
magnitude: Greenwald et al. (2014), the authors' summaries and re-analyses of their own studies; no intervals or test statistics printed. Availability, % of placebo, 4 hours after the daily dose: Zubieta et al. (2000; n = 3; liquid) 50–64% at 2 mg/day and 5–21% at 16 mg/day across regions; Greenwald et al. (2003; n = 5; tablets; range of means across seven regions) 53–72% at 2 mg, 9–20% at 16 mg, 2–12% at 32 mg; curve-fit estimates for doses not studied 71–85% (1 mg), 36–55% (4 mg), 20–35% (8 mg; 12–33% in the Fig. 1 legend), 13–24% (12 mg), 4–15% (24 mg). Comer et al. (2005; 7 on buprenorphine/naloxone against 8 on placebo; tested 15 hours after the dose; modelled from behaviour, not imaged): 21–31% (2/0.5 mg), 11–22% (8/2 mg), 6–12% (32/8 mg). After stopping 16 mg/day (Greenwald et al., 2007; n = 10): against the 2003 placebo condition 27–31% at 4 h, 54–61% at 28 h, 65–75% at 52 h and 77–94% at 76 h; adjusted curve estimates 13–25% (4 h), 19–30% (8 h), 24–36% (12 h), 29–41% (16 h), 37–46% (24 h), 56–73% (48 h), 75–90% (72 h); subjective effects of hydromorphone 24 mg intramuscularly significantly smaller at 4 and 28 h than at 52 and 76 h (no statistics printed). Variation between people (2003 study): coefficients of variation at 16 and 32 mg/day 24% and 21% for availability, 39% and 54% for plasma levels, 129% and 109% for withdrawal symptoms; a 3.5-fold range of availability at 2 mg/day in most regions. Heavier smokers (20 or more cigarettes a day, n = 5) had significantly lower availability than lighter smokers (15 or fewer, n = 5) in the 2007 study. Thresholds in the abstract and summary, inferences rather than measurements: withdrawal suppression at 50% availability or less (trough plasma level at least 1 ng/mL); blockade of typical doses below 20% (trough at least 3 ng/mL), from preliminary modelling; below 10% against higher-than-usual doses.

evidence.extracted: The authors use receptor availability (non-displaceable binding potential), an indirect measure, instead of 'occupancy', which they call misleading and not measurable directly in people; a fall in availability is proportional to a rise in occupancy only if receptor affinity and endogenous opioid levels are constant. Measures taken 4 hours after the daily dose, the earliest post-dose time studied, probably reflect less than the largest fall in availability; within-day PET time courses are not feasible. There is no gold-standard definition of clinically meaningful blockade, and neither the availability needed for withdrawal suppression or blockade nor how it varies with patients, opioids and routes is known.

risk_of_bias.note: Seen only through a narrative review by the authors of the studies (card sc_greenwald_2014: narrative-review checklist high; no search, the authors' own studies re-analysed by them). The primary studies cannot be appraised from the review; as it describes them, doses were given in a fixed order (2, 16, then 0 mg; 32, 16, 2, 0 mg), the time course after stopping is referenced to other people's placebo scans, the Comer estimates come from a model fitted to behaviour against a separate placebo group, and values between scans are curve fits.

inconsistency.note: The studies point the same way (availability falling with dose and rising after stopping; blockade incomplete at every dose studied); imaging and modelling give different figures, which the authors say should not be compared.

indirectness.note: Second-hand; volunteers dependent on heroin, not in treatment, mostly men, relatively healthy; fentanyl was not studied; receptor availability and laboratory self-administration stand in for what people ask (whether other opioids work, and the risk of using them), and no breathing or overdose outcome is reported.

imprecision.note: 3, 5 and 10 people in the scan studies and 7 against 8 in the modelling study; no intervals or tests are printed for any availability figure.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the review selected the authors' own studies.

grade.reasoning: As the review describes them, the primary studies are within-person comparisons with placebo given in a fixed order, a time course without a concurrent control and a comparison with a separate group, so the evidence starts low (METHODS 6.3: within-person laboratory studies start high only when the order was randomized or counterbalanced, and a claim seen only through reviews starts from the design of the primary studies). Down one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision: very low (the floor is reached at the first downgrade; the others are recorded for their reasons). The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft and its statement says the figures are second-hand (METHODS 6.3). Status replicated by the same team: the fall in availability with dose was seen in two scan studies (3 and 5 people) and incomplete blockade in several studies, all by overlapping authors; the time course after stopping rests on one study of 10 people. The abstract's thresholds are reported as the authors' inferences, not as findings. The doses are the studies' conditions; the claim gives no dosing advice and no timing for using other opioids.

statement: In people entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US treatment centres who said they had probably or definitely used fentanyl and who had taken buprenorphine after fentanyl, remembering severe withdrawal on taking it was common, and more common the shorter the shortest wait after fentanyl that people reported, in one self-report survey analysed without adjustment (Varshneya et al., 2022, read from the author manuscript). Of 1,679 people whose answers were collected at admission by an outcomes-tracking system, 1,163 (69.3%) reported fentanyl use; 421 of them had never taken buprenorphine after fentanyl and 57 had done so only with a shortest wait of 1 month to 1 year. Of the 685 whose shortest wait was under 1 month, 250 (36.5%; 95% CI 33.0 to 40.2, editors' calculation) said their withdrawal symptoms on taking buprenorphine after fentanyl had been severe, 136 (19.9%) moderate, 122 (17.8%) mild and 177 (25.8%) none; of 200 who had taken methadone after fentanyl, 30 (15.0%) said severe. Severe withdrawal after buprenorphine was remembered by 152 of the 339 people whose shortest wait was under 24 hours (44.8%) and 55 of the 160 whose shortest wait was 24 to 48 hours (34.4%), and, by the editors' reconstruction from the printed odds ratios (checked against the bars of Figure 1), by 25 of 97 at 48 to 72 hours (25.8%), 13 of 52 at 72 hours to 1 week (25.0%) and 5 of 37 at 1 week to 1 month (13.5%): a gradual fall, with no clear cut-off. The abstract's 22.19% for 'those who waited less than 24 hours' is 152 out of all 685, not out of the 339 who waited less than 24 hours (editors' calculation). The paper's odds ratios for severe withdrawal (under 24 hours 5.20, 95% CI 1.98 to 13.68; 24 to 48 hours 3.35, 1.24 to 9.09; 48 to 72 hours 2.22, 0.78 to 6.33; 72 hours to 1 week 2.13, 0.69 to 6.62) are unadjusted and compare each group with a reference the paper does not name, which the editors' exact reproduction shows to be the 37 people whose shortest wait was 1 week to 1 month; the results call the odds ratios of about 2 at 48 hours to 1 week no increase, and the conclusion compares with everyone who waited more than 48 hours, which the model did not do. The answers were remembered when people entered treatment, about one or more unspecified occasions; the shortest wait ever was not tied to the occasion of the withdrawal; the survey did not record the dose, form, setting or supervision of the buprenorphine, or whether withdrawal had begun before it was taken; and a single rating cannot tell withdrawal that buprenorphine brought on from withdrawal it did not relieve (the authors explain severe withdrawal after methadone as too little opioid effect early in treatment). The survey period, response rate, full questionnaire and centres are not described, and the descriptive appendix was not on file. Among the 152 people who had taken both medicines after fentanyl, 69 (45.4%) remembered severe withdrawal after buprenorphine and 20 (13.2%) after methadone. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Can Suboxone put you in withdrawal if you use fentanyl? Many people say it did. In a survey of people starting treatment at 49 US centres who said they used fentanyl, 250 of 685 who had taken buprenorphine (the main medicine in Suboxone) after fentanyl remembered severe withdrawal when they took it, 37 in 100, against 15 in 100 of those who had taken methadone after fentanyl. The shorter the shortest wait after fentanyl that people reported, the more often they remembered severe withdrawal: about 45 in 100 when it was under a day, 34 in 100 at one to two days, about 25 in 100 at two days to a week and 14 in 100 at a week to a month, with no clear cut-off. These are memories collected when people started treatment, about occasions nobody recorded. The survey did not know the dose, the form or who gave it, it allowed for nothing else that differed between people, and one question cannot tell withdrawal that buprenorphine brought on from withdrawal it failed to relieve. The paper's own summary gives 22 in 100 for those who waited under a day, but that is out of all 685 people, not out of the 339 who waited that little.
population: People entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US treatment centres using one outcomes-tracking system (survey period and centres not described) whose main drug was opioids and who said they had probably or definitely used fentanyl before treatment: 1,163 of 1,679 (mean age 30.8 years; 70.6% men; 80.4% White; 43.9% said their urine tested positive for fentanyl at admission); withdrawal ratings analysed for the 685 whose shortest wait after fentanyl before buprenorphine was under 1 month and for 200 who had taken methadone after fentanyl
exposure: Taking buprenorphine after fentanyl (any product; the table note names seven brands, Suboxone among them), grouped by the shortest time people said they had ever waited after fentanyl: under 24 hours, 24 to 48 hours, 48 to 72 hours, 72 hours to 1 week, 1 week to 1 month; dose, form, setting and supervision not recorded
comparator: Shorter against longer shortest waits (reference, by the editors' reproduction of the printed odds ratios: the 37 people whose shortest wait was 1 week to 1 month); methadone taken after fentanyl (200 people; 199 in the odds model); no adjustment for anything
outcome: Self-rated withdrawal symptoms on taking buprenorphine (or methadone) after fentanyl, remembered at treatment entry (none, mild, moderate or severe; one item, not a validated scale); the authors take severe withdrawal after buprenorphine as precipitated withdrawal
magnitude: Varshneya et al. (2022), Table 1 and text. Fentanyl use reported by 1,163 of 1,679 (69.3%; probably 180, definitely 983). Shortest wait before buprenorphine (of 1,163): under 24 h 339 (29.1%), 24–48 h 160 (13.8%), 48–72 h 97 (8.3%), 72 h–1 week 52 (4.5%), 1 week–1 month 37 (3.2%), 1 month–1 year 57 (4.9%), never 421 (36.2%); methadone 135, 22, 21, 13, 8, 29 and 935. evidence.locator: Abstract, Methods (p. 1); Methods › Sample and Assessments; Methods › Statistical Analyses (p. 2)
evidence.extracted: Self-report data from 1,679 people entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US treatment facilities, collected by a third-party aggregation system (Trac9) to track treatment outcomes at routine admission and received de-identified. People whose primary drug was opioids and who reported probably or definitely using fentanyl were asked whether they had used buprenorphine (or methadone, as a comparator) after fentanyl, the time between the two, and whether the medicine relieved or worsened their withdrawal. Severe withdrawal was analysed by binary logistic regression; descriptive statistics are in Appendix 1 (not on file). No survey period, centre description or response rate is given.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_varshneya_2022 (JBI prevalence checklist; editors' summary high): answers remembered at treatment entry about unspecified occasions, one unvalidated self-rating, sample frame, period and response rate not described, the shortest wait ever not tied to the occasion of the withdrawal, no adjustment, and headline percentages with the wrong denominators.

inconsistency.note: One survey; no conflicting data were read.

indirectness.note: The outcome measured (severe withdrawal remembered on taking buprenorphine after fentanyl) is not the same as withdrawal brought on by buprenorphine, which a single rating cannot separate from withdrawal it did not relieve; dose, form and setting are unknown, so nothing transfers to supervised starts.

imprecision.note: The overall share is precise (33.0% to 40.2%), but the gradient is measured against a reference group of 37 people with 5 severe ratings (odds ratio under 24 hours 1.98 to 13.68; the ratios at 48 hours to 1 week include 1).

grade.reasoning: A cross-sectional self-report survey starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision: very low (the floor is reached at the first downgrade; the others are recorded for their reasons). Rated as worded: how often people entering treatment who said they used fentanyl remembered severe withdrawal after taking buprenorphine following fentanyl, and its association with the shortest wait they reported. It cannot give the incidence of withdrawal brought on by buprenorphine, or show that waiting longer prevents it, and no gradient was used to upgrade (unadjusted, self-reported groups). Status: single study; the paper cites only case reports and anecdotal accounts as earlier evidence. The waiting times appear only as the survey's groups, never as advice.

statement: In US Medicaid enrollees aged 18 to 64 who stopped buprenorphine after 6 to 18 months of continuous treatment and stayed enrolled for the next 6 months, about 5 in 100 had at least one medically treated drug overdose, and between 4 and 5 in 10 visited an emergency department, in the 6 months after stopping, in one claims-based cohort study with no group that stayed on treatment (Williams et al., 2020, read from the online-first version). In the MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims of 2013–2017, 8,996 people met these conditions (61.0% women, 91.5% White, 76.4% aged 25 to 44; mean starting dose 8.0 mg a day). Stopping meant a gap of more than 60 days after the last prescription's supply ran out, and the 6 months were counted from the last day of supply. In those 6 months, 464 people (5.2%; 95% CI 4.7 to 5.6, editors' calculation) had at least one medically treated overdose, opioid or non-opioid (5.1% to 5.5% in the four groups by length of treatment; 5.6% among the 8,077 with a recorded diagnosis of opioid use disorder); 41.2% to 48.6% had at least one emergency department visit, 11.3% to 13.9% at least one hospital admission, and 19.1% to 25.9% filled a prescription for a full-agonist opioid, which the authors read as a marker of relapse or poorly coordinated care. Against people treated for 6 to 9 months (4,126), those treated for 15 to 18 months (931) had lower adjusted odds of emergency visits (odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.86), hospital admission (0.79, 0.64 to 0.99) and opioid prescriptions (0.67, 0.56 to 0.80), and those treated for 12 to 15 months lower odds of emergency visits (0.84) and opioid prescriptions (0.84), but the odds of overdose did not differ (15 to 18 months 1.04, 0.75 to 1.44, an interval that allows odds about 25% lower to 44% higher, editors' reading). Overdose after stopping was more likely with a recorded psychiatric diagnosis (odds ratio 1.61), alcohol use disorder (2.02) or another drug use disorder (1.51), and less likely in women (0.65). Because no group continued buprenorphine, the study cannot say whether stopping raised these risks compared with staying on treatment; the records do not say why anyone stopped; and the comparison of durations is adjusted only for age, sex, race, plan type, recorded diagnoses and starting dose, which the authors say leaves residual confounding possible. Deaths are not recorded: anyone who died, or lost Medicaid for any other reason, in the 6 months after stopping was excluded (3,940 of the 12,936 who stopped within the study window, 30.5%, editors' calculation), so fatal overdoses are not counted, as the authors say, and the figures are not the full risk after stopping. Only overdoses billed to Medicaid were counted, and the code list is printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50, which leaves out T40.0 to T40.4, the codes for poisoning by opium, heroin, methadone and other opioids (study card note), although the same sentence says that opioid overdoses were counted; the codes used are in an online table (S1) that was not on file. The people studied had all stayed in treatment at least 6 months, a minority the authors describe as likely relatively stable, so the figures may not apply to people who stop in the first weeks or months, or outside Medicaid. The discussion's statement that overdose rates after stopping are two to three times those of a general sample of people with opioid use disorder gives no figures and sets this study's medically treated overdoses beside death rates from another study, so it is not used here. Death rates during and after methadone or buprenorphine treatment, from a review of cohort studies, are a separate answer (see the answer on whether it is dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: What happens after stopping Suboxone? In US Medicaid records of 8,996 people who stopped buprenorphine (the main medicine in Suboxone) after 6 to 18 months of treatment, about 5 in 100 had at least one overdose treated by a doctor or hospital in the next 6 months. In those 6 months, 41 to 49 in 100 went to an emergency department, 11 to 14 in 100 stayed in hospital, and 19 to 26 in 100 filled a prescription for another opioid. People who had been on buprenorphine for 15 to 18 months had fewer emergency visits, hospital stays and opioid prescriptions afterwards than people who stopped after 6 to 9 months, but no fewer overdoses. Nobody in the study stayed on treatment, so it cannot say whether stopping raised the risk, and the records do not say why people stopped. People who died, or lost their Medicaid cover, in those 6 months were left out, so overdoses that killed people are not counted. Deaths during and after treatment are covered in a separate answer.
population: Adults aged 18 to 64 in the MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims database (2013–2017; contributing states not named) who began a new buprenorphine episode for opioid use disorder, stayed on it continuously for 6 to 18 months, then stopped, and stayed enrolled in Medicaid for the 6 months afterwards: 8,996 people (61.0% women; 91.5% White; 76.4% aged 25 to 44; mean starting dose 8.0 mg a day); people also covered by Medicare were excluded
exposure: Stopping buprenorphine (a gap of more than 60 days after the last prescription's supply ran out) after 6–9 (4,126 people), 9–12 (2,440), 12–15 (1,499) or 15–18 months (931) of continuous treatment, by days supplied in pharmacy claims; the 6 months of follow-up counted from the last day of supply
comparator: No group that continued buprenorphine. The longer-treatment groups against the 6–9-month group, adjusted for age, sex, race (White or not), Medicaid plan type, recorded psychiatric, alcohol and other drug use disorder diagnoses, and starting dose
outcome: At least one medically treated drug overdose, opioid or non-opioid (ICD-10 codes printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50), at least one emergency department visit, at least one inpatient admission, and at least one filled full-agonist opioid prescription, in Medicaid claims in the 6 months after stopping; deaths not recorded
magnitude: Williams et al. (2020). Flow: 26,576 with a new continuous episode of more than 6 months; 10,481 who did not stop (39.4%, editors) and 3,159 who stopped too late in the study window removed; 12,936 who stopped within the window; 3,940 (30.5%, editors) removed for incomplete enrolment in the 6 months after stopping; 8,996 analysed (6–9 months 4,126; 9–12 months 2,440; 12–15 months 1,499; 15–18 months 931). Six-month outcomes across the four groups, unadjusted: emergency department visit 41.2–48.6% (abstract 42.1–49.9%), inpatient admission 11.3–13.9%, full-agonist opioid prescription 19.1–25.9%, medically treated overdose 5.1–5.5%; overall overdose 464/8,996 = 5.2% (Wilson 95% CI 4.7–5.6, editors). 15–18 against 6–9 months, unadjusted: emergency visits 41.2% against 48.6% (p < 0.001), admissions 11.3% against 13.9% (p < 0.05), opioid prescriptions 19.1% against 25.9% (p < 0.001). Adjusted odds ratios against 6–9 months (Table 2): 15–18 months, admission 0.79 (0.64–0.99), emergency visit 0.75 (0.65–0.86), overdose 1.04 (0.75–1.44), opioid prescription 0.67 (0.56–0.80); 12–15 months 0.86 (0.72–1.03), 0.84 (0.75–0.95), 1.10 (0.84–1.43), 0.84 (0.73–0.97); 9–12 months 0.86 (0.74–1.01), 0.94 (0.85–1.04), 1.04 (0.82–1.30), 0.95 (0.85–1.07). Overdose, other terms in the same model: women 0.65 (0.54–0.79); psychiatric diagnosis 1.61 (1.32–1.96); alcohol use disorder 2.02 (1.47–2.79); non-opioid drug use disorder 1.51 (1.22–1.86); starting dose 1.00 per mg (0.97–1.04). Sensitivity analysis (8,077 with a recorded opioid use disorder diagnosis): 15–18 against 6–9 months, emergency visits 0.74 (0.64–0.86), admissions 0.79 (0.63–0.99), opioid prescriptions 0.68 (0.56–0.82); odds of overdose equivalent across groups, 5.6% overall.

evidence.extracted: MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims, 2013–2017, about 12 million enrollees a year. Adults aged 18–64 starting a new buprenorphine episode (no buprenorphine claim in the previous 60 days; formulations for pain excluded), continuously on it for at least 180 days and continuously enrolled for 6 months after stopping; buprenorphine started before 1 January 2017. Stopping was a gap of more than 60 days beyond the days supplied by the last fill, dated to the last day of medication coverage. Groups by days supplied: 6–9 months (180–270 days), 9–12 (271–364), 12–15 (365–455) and 15–18 (456–545); the 6–9-month group is the reference.

evidence.extracted: The authors state that residual confounding remains possible and that the severity of the disorder could not be measured from claims; that the sample likely represents relatively stable patients, a minority of Medicaid patients who reach 6 months of treatment, and likely differs from the many who stop in the first weeks or months; that without data on vital status fatal and non-fatal overdoses could not be told apart, and people who died of overdose during treatment or in the 6 months after stopping would have lost Medicaid eligibility and been ineligible for the analysis; that results are limited to Medicaid enrollees without Medicare and may not generalize; and that the design cannot establish a causal relationship between longer treatment and outcomes.

risk_of_bias.note: Coverage and measurement could change the figures materially (card sc_williams_2020, ROBINS-I serious): 3,940 of the 12,936 who stopped (30.5%) were excluded for losing Medicaid in the 6 months after stopping, a group that includes everyone who died; overdoses count only if billed to Medicaid; the printed code list leaves out the opioid codes, and the table of the codes used was not read.

inconsistency.note: One study; the four duration groups give similar overdose rates (5.1% to 5.5%).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: Medicaid enrollees who stopped after at least 6 months and stayed enrolled; the statement says the figures leave out deaths, may not apply to people who stop early or are outside Medicaid, and come with no group that stayed on treatment.

imprecision.note: 464 overdoses; the overall share has a narrow interval (4.7% to 5.6%). The duration comparison for overdose is imprecise (0.75 to 1.44) and is worded as no detected difference.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; all four outcomes are reported for every comparison, including the null overdose result.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (how many people had each event in the 6 months after stopping): starts low; down one level for risk of bias, because exclusions that include every death and an overdose definition that cannot be checked could change the figures materially: very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded. The comparisons by length of treatment are associations in the same records, open to confounding by why and when people stopped, and are not rated separately; the authors concede the design cannot show cause. Nothing here compares stopping with continuing: deaths during and after treatment are the subject of the answer on whether it is dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine, which rests on a review of cohort studies and measures deaths, not treated overdoses; the two do not conflict. Status: single study.

verification.flag_note: Question 16 of round pdf-2026-11-26. Read from the online-first version (AJP in Advance, 8 pages); the print version (Am J Psychiatry 177(2), 117–124) was not read, and the online supplement (Tables S1 to S3: overdose codes, diagnosis codes, sensitivity analysis) was not on file: Table S1 would settle the code list. Not read: Larochelle et al. (2018), Annals of Internal Medicine 169, 137–145, the source of the authors' comparison with annual rates after a past overdose. Whether stopping raises the risk would need a cohort that links deaths and includes people who stay on buprenorphine. Kept consistent with the answer on deaths during and after methadone or buprenorphine treatment (Sordo et al., 2017), which this claim points to and does not repeat.
